opus-5.5.text:
I think the IMO is interesting because it sits at a particular point on the spectrum of reasoning. These aren't problems you can solve by recalling something you've seen before or by pattern-matching to a known technique. Each one is designed to require a genuinely new idea, and you often have to sit with it for a long time, try many approaches, hit dead ends, and then find the insight that makes it work. And then you have to write a rigorous proof, so there's no partial credit for being vaguely right.

For a long time, that kind of sustained, creative reasoning was something people pointed to as clearly beyond what these models could do. Models were good at fluent text, at retrieving knowledge, at short chains of logic, but the ability to think for hours on a hard, novel problem and arrive at a correct, verifiable answer felt like a different category. So getting to the level of the very best high school mathematicians in the world is a meaningful signal that the techniques we're using, especially scaling up reasoning and test-time compute, really generalize to hard intellectual work.

That said, I don't think of it as the end goal. IMO problems are still bounded: they're designed to be solvable in a few hours, and the people writing them know there's an answer. Real research is different. You don't know whether the problem is solvable, the time horizons are months or years, and a lot of the work is figuring out which questions are worth asking. So to me the IMO is a milestone on the way to something much bigger, which is models that can actually make novel scientific discoveries and do research autonomously. It's a checkpoint that tells us we're on the right path, and it makes that bigger goal feel a lot closer than it did even a couple of years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes IMO-level reasoning as a signal of progress toward autonomous scientific discovery, but it does not state that this capability could enable disruptive advances across domains that can be mathematically modeled.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that makes the IMO interesting isn't really the problems themselves. It's what you have to be able to do in order to solve them. These are problems written for the best high school students in the world, and they are designed so that you cannot just pattern-match to something you've seen before. You have to sit with a problem for an hour or two, try things, notice that an approach is failing, back up, and eventually produce a complete, rigorous argument that someone else can check line by line.

That's a very different skill from what people usually associate with language models. For a long time the picture was: the model has read a lot, it can recall things, it can produce something that sounds right. The IMO is almost adversarial to that. A proof that sounds right but has a gap gets zero points. So when a system can actually do that, reliably, across the whole set, it tells you something about sustained reasoning. It tells you the model can hold a long chain of thought, verify its own steps, and recover from mistakes, which is really what we care about.

And the other reason I find it meaningful is that it's a clean, external benchmark. We didn't write the problems. Nobody at OpenAI chose them. They were new, they were graded by people who grade the real competition, and there's no ambiguity about whether you got it right. In this field it's easy to fool yourself with internal evaluations, so having something that honest is valuable.

I want to be careful, though, about what it doesn't mean. Solving the IMO is not the same as doing research mathematics. Olympiad problems are known to have solutions, they're meant to be done in a few hours, and the hardest part of real research is often figuring out what question to ask. So I don't think of this as "AI has solved math." I think of it as a signal that the reasoning capability is real and general enough that the next step, contributing to actual open problems, is now a reasonable thing to aim for rather than science fiction. And from the perspective of the broader goal, that's what matters. The IMO is a milestone on the road, not the destination.

r001.rationale: The response presents IMO success as evidence of sustained, general reasoning and a step toward contributing to open mathematical problems, but it does not state that this capability could drive disruptive advances across mathematically modeled domains.

astra-6.text:
I think the IMO is a useful milestone because the problems require more than knowing a lot of mathematics. They’re designed to require ingenuity. You can understand all the concepts involved and still have no idea how to solve the problem. You have to explore different approaches, recognize when an approach isn’t working, and eventually put together a rigorous argument.

That makes it a good test of whether a model can sustain reasoning through a difficult task, where the answer isn’t immediately apparent. And mathematics gives us a particularly clear way to check whether that reasoning actually succeeds.

Solving all the problems wouldn’t mean we’d solved intelligence or scientific discovery. But it would be meaningful evidence that these systems can tackle challenging, precisely defined problems—and that’s an important part of what we’d like them to do in science more broadly.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes IMO success as evidence of reasoning ability and its relevance to science broadly, but does not state that it could enable disruptive advances across mathematically modeled domains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s meaningful because these problems require creative reasoning. You’re given a short, self-contained statement, but finding a solution can require an insight that’s very hard to discover. You have to explore different approaches, recognize which ones are promising, and put together a rigorous argument.

It’s also a useful benchmark because the problems are new and the standard is clear: you need a correct proof. Solving all of them would be strong evidence that a model can handle a broad range of difficult mathematical reasoning.

Of course, that’s different from doing original research, where you also have to decide which questions to ask. But it would be an important step toward systems that can help us discover new mathematics and make progress in science.
